props.title: Dressed to Kill
props.initialSlug: A psychiatrist's patient leads a deadly double life

sections.content: Brian De Palma's Dressed to Kill (1980) masterfully channels Hitchcockian suspense through a lurid, psychosexual lens. Like Psycho (1960), it opens with a shocking murder of its apparent protagonist - here, Angie Dickinson's sexually frustrated Kate Miller. The infamous museum sequence, where Kate plays cat-and-mouse with a mysterious stranger, demonstrates De Palma's virtuosic camera movement and split-screen techniques that defined his 1970s-80s thriller peak alongside Body Double (1984) and Blow Out (1981).

sections.content: The film's treatment of gender and identity sparked intense controversy, particularly in its portrayal of psychiatrist Dr. Robert Elliott (Michael Caine) and the killer's psychological motivations. While problematic by today's standards, it reflects similar themes explored in The Silence of the Lambs (1991) and Basic Instinct (1992) - thrillers that merged psychological complexity with explicit content and drew both praise and criticism for their depiction of gender-nonconforming antagonists.

Nancy Allen's performance as Liz Blake, a high-class escort who becomes amateur detective, channels the "investigating woman in peril" archetype seen in films like Klute (1971) and Eyes of Laura Mars (1978). De Palma's signature split-screen sequences and dreamlike atmosphere reach their apex in the museum and subway scenes, displaying the technical mastery that influenced later erotic thrillers like Fatal Attraction (1987). sections.content: Dressed to Kill helped establish the template for the sophisticated erotic thriller that would dominate the late 1980s and early 1990s. Its blend of sexuality, violence, and psychological complexity paved the way for films like Sea of Love (1989) and In the Cut (2003). De Palma's technical flourishes - particularly his use of split-screen, slow motion, and subjective camera work - influenced countless imitators but were rarely matched in their artistic execution.
